title: Pot-au-Feu
subtitle: The French national dish: beef and vegetables simmered in their own broth
excerpt: France's great national dish: a whole piece of beef and bone marrow simmered slowly with root vegetables and aromatics until the broth is crystal-clear and deep with flavour. Served in two courses: the broth first, then the meat and vegetables.

recipe.sourceNotes: Pot-au-feu (literally pot on the fire) is described by Auguste Escoffier and virtually every major French culinary authority as the symbol of French domestic cooking, a national dish in the truest sense. The dish is essentially a method rather than a fixed recipe: a large cut of beef and sometimes a boiling fowl or marrow bones are simmered over very low heat in water for several hours, with root vegetables and a bouquet garni added partway through. The resulting broth is served first as a starter, often with toast or vermicelli, then the meat and vegetables follow as the main course, accompanied by coarse salt, Dijon mustard, cornichons, and horseradish. The marrow bones, when included, are scooped with a small spoon and eaten on toasted bread. Pot-au-feu is related to the Spanish cocido, the Italian bollito misto, and the British boiled beef and carrots.

recipeTools.notes: A very large stockpot of at least 8 litres capacity.

content.text: Start the beef in cold water and bring it up slowly; this draws the proteins into the broth rather than sealing them inside, producing a cleaner, more flavourful broth at the cost of slightly drier meat. Skim diligently in the first 30 minutes: the grey foam is coagulated protein that makes the broth cloudy and slightly bitter if left. The broth should barely tremble throughout the cooking: a rolling boil will make it cloudy.

content.text: Place the beef brisket and beef shin in a very large pot and cover with 3 litres of cold water. Bring slowly to a simmer over medium heat, skimming the foam as it rises. Once clear, add the charred onion, garlic, cloves, thyme, bay leaves, and parsley stalks. Season lightly. Simmer with the lid ajar at the merest tremble for 2.5 to 3 hours.

After 2 hours, add the carrots, turnips, leeks, and celery to the broth. Continue cooking for 45 minutes to 1 hour until the vegetables are tender and the beef is very soft when pierced with a skewer. Season the broth to taste with salt.

Lift out the meat and vegetables and keep warm. Strain the broth through a fine sieve and serve it first in bowls with toasted bread. Then serve the sliced beef and vegetables with Dijon mustard, coarse sea salt, and cornichons.
